relevance.reason: A continental digital-trade protocol whose objectives expressly include emerging and advanced technologies (Article 2(2)(f)) and which has an Annex on Emerging and Advanced Technologies. The Annex is not merely cooperative: Article 4 requires each State Party to facilitate deployment and not to deny market access solely because a person uses emerging technologies; Article 5 imposes a national-treatment obligation; Article 12 requires technical standards and regulations for safe, responsible and ethical deployment and their harmonisation. The Protocol is binding once in force, but entry into force is not confirmed.

related.note: Both documents assert sovereignty and a UN-centred framework; the BRICS statement is a collective leaders' text, whereas China's initiative is a unilateral government proposal.
The BRICS statement precedes WAICO by a year and expresses a similar Global South capacity-building position, but it creates no institution and has no formal link to WAICO.
Both are non-binding summit statements with a development and access agenda; New Delhi is a wider summit declaration, while the BRICS statement is a coalition statement.
The UN's Global Digital Compact is the universal digital-cooperation framework; the BRICS statement is a separate coalition text that calls for the UN to be at the core of AI governance.

ai_provisions: Digital sovereignty and the right to development — all countries may adopt their own AI regulatory frameworks, develop AI capacities and pursue technological autonomy within their jurisdictions.
Global governance under the UN Charter — AI governance must respect national sovereignty, be representative, development-oriented, accessible and inclusive, and place the United Nations at its core.
Market regulation and data governance — personal data protection, information integrity and the rights and interests of humanity.
AI for sustainable development — innovation, productivity, sustainable practices and the reduction of digital and data divides within and between countries.
Capacity building — support for developing countries, technology transfer and access to AI technologies and skills.
Risk mitigation — collective action on safety, transparency, accountability and the risks arising from AI, without creating binding obligations.
International cooperation — the statement warns that a proliferation of initiatives and diverging views may aggravate asymmetries and the legitimacy gap in global digital governance.
relevance.excluded_scope: A political statement by BRICS leaders. It creates no binding obligation, no signature or ratification, no depositary, no monitoring or reporting duty and no dispute-settlement mechanism. It does not establish an institution or a follow-up mechanism. National implementation is not assessed.
relevance.reason: The first stand-alone BRICS leaders' statement on the global governance of artificial intelligence, adopted at the 17th BRICS Summit in Rio de Janeiro on 6 July 2025 by the leaders of the 11 BRICS member States. It sets out a collective position centred on digital sovereignty, the right to development, the UN Charter, capacity building and the concerns of the Global South. It is a political statement, not a treaty: it creates no legal obligation, ratification, depositary or monitoring. It is included because it is a distinct coalition instrument that the three-pole reading would otherwise miss, and because it documents the China-Global South diffusion position before WAICO was established.

Peru — Declaration contained in the instrument of accession and in a Note Verbale from the Embassy of Peru in France, received and registered at the Secretariat General on 26 August 2019 – Or. Engl.

DECLARATIONS ACCORDING TO ARTICLE 40 OF THE CONVENTION

In accordance with Article 2 of the Convention on Cybercrime, the Republic of Peru declares that its national law requires the offense of illegal access to be committed in violation of security measures.

In accordance with Article 3 of the Convention on Cybercrime, the Republic of Peru declares that its national law requires the offense of illegal interception is committed with criminal intent and that such offense may be committed in relation to a computer system connected to another computer system.

In accordance with Article 7 of the Convention on Cybercrime, the Republic of Peru declares that it may require that a similar fraudulent or criminal intent exists, in accordance with the provisions of its national law, so that the conduct described in that article engenders a criminal responsibility.

In accordance with Article 27, paragraph 9, sub-paragraph (e) of the Convention on Cybercrime, the Republic of Peru declares that in the interest of efficiency, the requests made under provisions of Article 27, paragraph 9, of the Convention should be addressed to its Central Authority.

Portugal — Declaration contained in the instrument of ratification deposited on 24 March 2010 - Or. Engl.

In accordance with Article 24, paragraph 5, of the Convention, the Portuguese Republic declares that it shall not grant extradition of persons who:

a) are to be trialled by an exceptional court or who are to serve a sentence passed by such a court;
b) it has been proved will be subject to a trial which affords no legal guarantees of criminal proceedings complying with the conditions internationally recognised as essential to the protection of human rights, or will serve their sentences in inhuman conditions;
c) are being demanded in connection with an offence punishable with a lifetime sentence or a lifetime detention order.

The Portuguese Republic shall grant extradition only for crimes punishable with penalty of deprivation of liberty superior to one year.

The Portuguese Republic shall not grant extradition of Portuguese nationals.

Portugal shall not grant extradition for offences punishable with the death penalty under the law of the requesting State.

Portugal shall authorise transit through its national territory only in respect of persons whose circumstances are such that their extradition may be granted.

The Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Ukraine presents its compliments to the Secretary General of the Council of Europe, as the Depositary of the European Convention on Information on Foreign Law of 7 June 1968, the Additional Protocol to the European Convention on Information on Foreign Law of 15 March 1978, the European Convention on the Supervision of Conditionally Sentenced or Conditionally Protocol to the European Convention on Extradition of 17 March 1978, the European Convention on the Suppression of Terrorism of 27 January 1977, the Protocol amending the European Convention on the committed through Computer Systems of 28 January 2003, the Convention on Laundering, Search, Seizure and Confiscation of the Proceeds from Crime of 8 November 1990, the Council of Europe Convention on Laundering, Search, Seizure and Confiscation of the Proceeds from Crime and on the Financing of Terrorism of 16 May 2005, the Council of Europe Convention on Action against Trafficking in Human Beings of 16 May 2005, the European Convention on the Exercise of Children's Rights of 25 January 1996, the Convention on Contact concerning Children of 15 May 2003, the European Convention on Recognition and Enforcement of Decisions concerning Custody of Children and on Restoration of Custody of Children of 20 May 1980, the Council of Europe Convention on the Protection of Children against Sexual Exploitation and Sexual Abuse of 25 October 2007, the Convention on the Establishment of a Scheme of Registration of Wills of 16 May 1972, the Agreement on Illicit Traffic by Sea, implementing Article 17 of the United Nations Convention against Illicit Traffic in Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances of 31 January 1995, the Criminal Law Convention on Corruption of 27 January 1999, the Additional Protocol to the Criminal Law Convention on Corruption of 15 May 2003 (hereinafter referred to as the «Conventions, Protocols, Agreement» respectively), and has the honour to inform of the following.

In February 2014 the Russian Federation launched armed aggression against Ukraine and occupied a part of the territory of Ukraine – the Autonomous Republic of Crimea and the city of Sevastopol, and today exercises effective control over certain districts of the Donetsk and Luhansk oblasts of Ukraine. These actions are in gross violation of the Charter of the United Nations and constitute a threat to international peace and security. The Russian Federation, as the Aggressor State and Occupying Power, bears full responsibility for its actions and their consequences under international law.

The United Nations General Assembly Resolution A/RES/68/262 of 27 March 2014 confirmed the sovereignty and territorial integrity of Ukraine within its internationally recognized borders. The United Nations also called upon all States, international organizations and specialized agencies not to recognize any alteration of the status of the Autonomous Republic of Crimea and the city of Sevastopol.

In this regard, Ukraine states that from 20 February 2014 and for the period of temporary occupation by the Russian Federation of a part of the territory of Ukraine – the Autonomous Republic of Crimea and the city of Sevastopol – as a result of the armed aggression of the Russian Federation committed against Ukraine and until the complete restoration of the constitutional law and order and effective control by Ukraine over such occupied territory, as well as over certain districts of the Donetsk and Luhansk oblasts of Ukraine, which are temporarily not under control of Ukraine as a result of the aggression of the Russian Federation, the application and implementation by Ukraine of the obligations under the above Conventions, Protocols, Agreement, as applied to the aforementioned occupied and uncontrolled territory of Ukraine, is limited and is not guaranteed.

Documents or requests made or issued by the occupying authorities of the Russian Federation, its officials at any level in the Autonomous Republic of Crimea and the city of Sevastopol and by the illegal authorities in certain districts of the Donetsk and Luhansk oblasts of Ukraine, which are temporarily not under control of Ukraine, are null and void and have no legal effect regardless of whether they are presented directly or indirectly through the authorities of the Russian Federation.

The provisions of the Conventions, Protocols, Agreement regarding the possibility of direct communication or interaction do not apply to the territorial organs of Ukraine in the Autonomous Republic of Crimea and the city of Sevastopol, as well as in certain districts of the Donetsk and Luhansk oblasts of Ukraine, which are temporarily not under control of Ukraine. The order of the relevant communication is determined by the central authorities of Ukraine in Kyiv.

Norway — Reservation and declarations contained in the instrument of ratification and in a Note verbale from the Permanent Representation of Norway, deposited simultaneously on 30 June 2006 – Or. Engl.

Pursuant to Article 14, paragraph 3, of the Convention, the Government of the Kingdom of Norway, reserves the right not to apply the measures referred to in Article 20 – Real-time collection of traffic data, in cases of less serious offences.

Clarification of what is meant by "less serious offences"
Pursuant to Article 14, paragraph 3, the Parties may reserve the right to apply the measures set out in Article 20 only to offences or categories of offences specified in the reservation. It is indicated in the Norwegian reservation, that Norway does not wish to allow the collection of traffic data in real time in connection with minor offences.
Section 216b of the Norwegian Criminal Procedure Act provides for the collection of traffic data in cases where there is just cause for suspecting a person of having committed an offence, or of having attempted to commit an offence, that is punishable by imprisonment for a term of five years or more, or of having contravened specific penal provisions.
The use of various types of communication control and other privacy-invasive coercive measures is primarily restricted to cases involving serious offences, where serious offences are defined as carrying a penalty of five or more years' imprisonment.

Clarification of the relationship between the reservation and the application of Articles 20 and 21 in Norwegian law
The right to apply the measures referred to in Article 20 only to offences specified in the reservation is conditional on the range of offences to which Article 20 is applied not being more restricted than the range of offences to which the measures referred to in Article 21 apply. The condition set out in Article 14 must be interpreted to mean that the range of offences for which traffic data may be collected in real time must not be more restricted than the range of offences for which interception of content data is permitted.
Article 21 (Interception of content data) is governed in Norwegian law by section 216a of the Criminal Procedure Act, and Article 20 by section 216b of the Criminal Procedure Act. Section 216a has a prescribed penalty limit of ten or more years' imprisonment, while section 216b has a prescribed penalty limit of five years' imprisonment. This means that section 216a applies to a narrower range of offences than section 216b, and the condition of Article 14 is thus fulfilled. Norway is therefore entitled to enter a reservation in accordance with Article 14.

legal_nature.rationale: A Council of Europe framework convention with signature (Article 29), ratification, acceptance or approval, entry into force on the fifth instrument including three member States (Article 30), and a Conference of the Parties. It creates legal obligations for Parties and is a treaty, not a recommendation.

declarations: European Union, Article 3(1)(b): Declaration of the European Union on the Scope of Application with regard to private actors pursuant to Article 3 paragraph 1 subparagraph b of the Convention. Recalling the obligation under Article 3 paragraph 1 subparagraph b of the Convention to address risks and impacts arising from activities within the lifecycle of artificial intelligence systems by private actors to the extent not covered in subparagraph a of that provision in a manner conforming with the object and purpose of the Convention, the Union declares that it will apply the principles and obligations set forth in Chapters II to VI of the Convention to activities of private actors placing on the market, making available and using artificial intelligence systems in the European Union through the implementation of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 of the European Parliament and the Council of 13 June 2024 laying down harmonised rules on artificial intelligence and amending Regulations (EC) No 300/2008, (EU) No 167/2013, (EU) No 168/2013, (EU) 2018/858, (EU) 2018/1139 and (EU) 2019/2144 and Directives 2014/90/EU, (EU) 2016/797 and (EU) 2020/1828 (Artificial Intelligence Act). Other relevant Union acquis may also apply to these activities and contribute to the implementation of the principles and the obligations of the Convention. (Declaration contained in the instrument of approval handed over on 15 May 2026; original English.)

European Union, Article 32(1): Declaration of the European Union on the Territorial Scope of Application pursuant to Article 32 paragraph 1 of the Convention. Pursuant to Article 32 paragraph 1 of the Convention, the Union declares that, with regard to the competence of the Union, the Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence and Human Rights, Democracy and the Rule of Law is to apply to the territories in which the EU Treaties are applied pursuant to Article 52 of the Treaty on European Union and under the conditions laid down in, inter alia, Article 355 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union. (Original English.)

Norway, Article 3(1)(b): In accordance with Article 3, paragraph 1.b, of the Convention, the Kingdom of Norway declares that it shall apply the principles and obligations set forth in Chapters II to VI of this Convention to activities of private actors. (Declaration contained in the full powers of signature handed over on 5 September 2024; original English.)

Ukraine, Article 3(1)(b): In accordance with Article 3, paragraph 1.b, of the Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence and Human Rights, Democracy and the Rule of Law, Ukraine declares that it shall take other appropriate measures with respect to the activities of private entities not covered by Article 3, paragraph 1, subparagraph “a”, of the Convention in order to fulfill the obligation set forth in Article 3, paragraph 1, subparagraph “b”, of the Convention in a manner consistent with the object and purpose of the Convention. (Declaration contained in the full powers of signature handed over on 15 May 2025; original English/Ukrainian.)

Ukraine, Article 32(1): In accordance with Article 32, paragraph 1, of the Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence and Human Rights, Democracy and the Rule of Law, Ukraine declares that the Convention shall not apply to the territory of Ukraine temporarily occupied by the Russian Federation until the armed aggression of the Russian Federation against Ukraine is completely terminated, the territorial integrity of Ukraine is restored within the internationally recognized state border of Ukraine, Ukraine regains full control over the state border of Ukraine and the constitutional order is restored on the relevant territory of Ukraine. (Original English/Ukrainian.)

Seven pillars (Chakras) — democratising AI resources; economic growth and social good; secure and trusted AI; AI for science; access for social empowerment; human capital development; resilient, efficient and innovative AI systems.
Democratising AI resources — robust digital infrastructure and affordable access, with international cooperation on compute, data, models and skills.
Secure and trusted AI — trustworthy frameworks, risk management and respect for national sovereignty.
AI for science and for social empowerment — use of AI in research and public services, including for development priorities.
Human capital development — skilling and reskilling, including the Equitable AI Transitions Playbook produced with the International Labour Organization.
Complementarity with existing international initiatives — the declaration is to be read alongside, not instead of, other international and regional AI processes.

relevance.reason: The declaration adopted at the AI Impact Summit in New Delhi on 19 February 2026, the fourth summit in the series that began at Bletchley Park in 2023. The Press Information Bureau's annex lists 92 endorsers as of 5 March 2026: 90 States, the European Union and IFAD, the widest endorsement count among the summit declarations in the corpus. It marks the series' shift from AI safety to AI impact and development, and it is a political declaration, not a treaty: it creates no legal obligation, ratification, depositary, monitoring or dispute settlement. It is included because the corpus already catalogues the Bletchley, Seoul and Paris summit texts and would otherwise omit the 2026 stage of the same series.

related.note: The San Francisco Declaration is the operational follow-up to the 2025 Pax Silica Declaration and reaffirms cooperation on enforcing policies to protect sensitive technologies and critical infrastructure.
The US-led Pax Silica architecture is the counterpart to the China-initiated WAICO. The San Francisco Declaration is a political instrument; WAICO is a treaty establishing an organisation.
Both frame AI governance through national security and sovereignty, from opposite institutional positions: a US-led supply-chain coalition and a Chinese-initiated intergovernmental organisation.

ai_provisions: Common understanding of 'sensitive technologies' - goods, software, materials, knowledge, components and means of production essential to SI supply chains whose theft, illicit transfer or acquisition would confer a military or intelligence advantage or undue economic leverage

Common understanding of 'critical infrastructure' - physical and digital systems and assets underpinning SI supply chains, including ports, terminals, transport, communications, logistics, ICT and energy infrastructure, and the digital platforms that coordinate them
Economic security as national security - the signatories affirm that safeguarding these technologies and infrastructure is a shared endeavour among aligned partners

Working groups - the declaration resolves to establish five groups covering pro-innovation policy frameworks, SI adoption in key sectors, supply-chain cooperation, safe harbors and security hubs, and SI security and resilience
Reduction of dependencies - the text aims to reduce reliance on adversaries for critical minerals, AI models and semiconductors, and to address economic coercion and non-market policies
relevance.excluded_scope: A political declaration. It creates no legal obligation, no ratification, no depositary, no monitoring or dispute-settlement mechanism and no institution with legal personality. The working groups are commitments to cooperate, not treaty bodies. The declaration does not regulate AI models or products directly, and it does not impose supply-chain controls; those would require separate national measures. Participation is by invitation to Pax Silica participants, not universal.
relevance.reason: A signed political declaration on the security of the technologies and infrastructure underpinning advanced AI and 'super intelligence' supply chains. It is the operational follow-up to the 2025 Pax Silica Declaration and the first Pax Silica document to be signed by named governments rather than endorsed collectively. It belongs in the corpus because it converts a coalition statement into working groups on sensitive technologies, critical infrastructure, supply-chain security and resilience, while remaining non-binding. It is a declaration, not a treaty, and signature does not create legal obligations.

related.note: The resolution welcomes the Pact for the Future and the Global Digital Compact, including their commitment to international human-rights law throughout the life cycle of digital and emerging technologies.
The resolution welcomes the first Global Dialogue on AI Governance in July 2026 and takes note of the Independent International Scientific Panel's preliminary report.
The resolution recalls the UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of AI (23 November 2021).
CETS 225 is the binding AI-specific human-rights treaty; the HRC resolution is universal but non-binding.
Earlier UNGA AI resolution; the HRC resolution builds on the UN's AI-governance track.

ai_provisions: Operative paragraph 1 — recognises AI's potential to contribute to human rights and sustainable development, while acknowledging risks to the enjoyment of human rights.

Operative paragraph 2 — affirms that the design, development, deployment and use of AI must be consistent with international law, including international human rights law and international humanitarian law as applicable.

Operative paragraphs 3–7 — AI governance under human-rights law; legislative and regulatory measures; participation of developing countries; access to information; human dignity, equality, privacy, transparency, explainability, accountability, accessibility, human oversight and effective remedies.

Operative paragraph 8 — States should refrain from or cease uses of AI that cannot be operated consistently with international human rights law or that pose undue risks, including systems whose capabilities could reasonably be expected to cause loss of human control.

Operative paragraphs 9–10 — human-rights due diligence and impact assessments; meaningful human oversight, information, human review and effective remedies where AI plays a material role in decisions affecting rights.

Operative paragraphs 11–13 — freedom of opinion and expression, privacy, differentiated impacts on vulnerable groups, and the responsibility of business enterprises under the Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights.
Operative paragraphs 14–17 — AI literacy, international cooperation and capacity building, digital public goods and open models, and coherence among international initiatives.
Operative paragraphs 20–23 — a panel discussion at the 65th session on AI capacity building and the AI divide; an OHCHR report to the 66th session; the Council remains seized of the matter.
relevance.excluded_scope: A non-binding Human Rights Council resolution. It creates no signature, ratification, depositary, monitoring or enforcement mechanism, and it does not establish a military-AI prohibition. It applies existing human-rights obligations rather than creating new ones.
relevance.reason: A dedicated Human Rights Council resolution on the human-rights implications of artificial intelligence, adopted without a vote on 6 October 2026. It complements the General Assembly resolutions and CETS 225 by applying existing international human-rights law across the AI life cycle: discrimination, privacy, freedom of expression, human oversight, due diligence, remedies and capacity building. It is non-binding and creates no enforcement mechanism, but it is the Human Rights Council's principal AI-specific text and was missing from the corpus.

ai_provisions: Article 1 — establishes WAICO as an independent intergovernmental international organization with international legal personality
Article 2 — purposes: human-centric AI, international cooperation, bridging the AI divide, risk mitigation and trustworthy AI

Article 3 — functions, including capacity building, alignment of governance rules and technical standards, open-source cooperation and support for the UN framework; functions are limited exclusively to the civilian domain
Article 4 — principles: UN Charter, sovereignty, diversity of civilizations, equality, multilateralism and extensive consultation
Articles 5–8 — Council, decision-making, Secretariat and financing
Article 10 — membership open to all States; Founding Members are States that sign during the open-for-signature period

Article 11 — observer status for non-member States and intergovernmental organisations, subject to an application to the Secretariat and approval by the Council; observers may attend the plenary on invitation and have no vote
Article 14 — signature from 1 May to 31 July 2026; ratification, acceptance or approval; accession thereafter
Article 15 — entry into force on the third instrument of ratification, acceptance or approval
Article 18 — China as depositary; Arabic, Chinese, English, French, Russian and Spanish texts equally authentic
relevance.excluded_scope: Military AI is excluded: Article 3(2) limits the Organization's functions exclusively to the civilian domain. The Agreement establishes an organization and a cooperation framework; it does not itself set product rules, prohibitions, testing standards or a judicial dispute-settlement mechanism. Disputes are to be settled by consultation (Article 13).
relevance.reason: The constituent treaty of the first intergovernmental international organization specifically dedicated to artificial intelligence. It establishes WAICO as an independent intergovernmental organization with international legal personality, headquartered in Shanghai, with a Council and a Secretariat, and limits its functions exclusively to the civilian domain of AI (Article 3(2)). It is subject to ratification, acceptance or approval and enters into force on the deposit of the third such instrument (Article 15). It is a treaty, not a political declaration, and it is the second AI-specific treaty in the corpus alongside CETS 225. The article references were checked against the official Chinese text published by the National People's Congress.
